# Landscape metrics

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal" collapse="true" title="If you start from here..."}
Run the following code to load and create everything you'll need to run the examples in this section.
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(terra)
landscape_sempach <- rast("data/landcover_4.tif")
df_levels <- data.frame(id = 1:4, cover = c("settlement", "agriculture", "forest", "unproductive"))
levels(landscape_sempach) <- df_levels
```
:::

## Introduction

We first need to load the `landscapemetrics` package. This is the package we are going to use to compute landscape indices. Since the standard output of `landscapemetrics` is a tibble, we are also loading the `dplyr` package. This is not strictly needed since tibbles are also data frames, but the display will be a bit nicer.

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(landscapemetrics)
library(dplyr)
```

Since the computation time of some indices can be quite high on large landscapes, we are going to use a small simulated landscape provided by the package authors. It's a 30x30 square landscape with 3 land cover categories.

```{r}
landscape <- rast(landscape)
plot(landscape)
```

Before computing metrics, we first need to check that our input raster data is fulfilling all the requirements of `landscapemetrics`:

* The input raster is categorical (with a reasonable amount of categories)
* Categories are encoded using integer values
* The landscape uses a projected coordinate reference system (CRS)
* The CRS uses meters as a distance unit

We thus check our simulated landscape. As a comparison, we also check the landscape we were using in the previous sections.

```{r}
check_landscape(landscape)
check_landscape(landscape_sempach)
```

We get a warning for the simulated data set since the CRS is not defined and `landscapemetrics` cannot know if the data is projected and/or using meters as a distance unit. To remove the warning, we will assign a projected CRS (we'll use the one used in Switzerland) to the raster. This is not a problem here since we don't care about the true location of this raster. However, in a real analysis, you should always check that your data has the appropriate CRS.

```{r}
crs(landscape) <- "EPSG:2056"
check_landscape(landscape)
```

You can use the `list_lsm()` function to get a list of all the metrics provided by `landscapemetrics`. Using the `level` and `type` arguments, it is also possible to get only the metrics for a specific level (patch, class or landscape) or a specific type of metrics.

```{r}
list_lsm()
list_lsm(level = "class", type = "shape metric")
```

The last column shows name of the function used to compute the metrics. You can access the documentation of every metric with the `help()` (or `?`) function.

```{r}
#| eval: false
help(lsm_p_area)
?lsm_p_area
```


## Patch metrics

A patch is an area of continuous land cover, and this continuity is defined by the numbers of connected neighbors. Most (maybe even all, I didn't check) functions of `landscapmetrics` use 8 neighbors (queen's case) but you can choose to use only 4 neighbors (rook's case). This can have a strong influence on the number of delineated patches. The `show_patches()` function allows us to visualize the patches. Let's use it with the 2 different settings.

```{r}
show_patches(landscape, directions = 4, labels = TRUE)
show_patches(landscape, directions = 8, labels = TRUE)
```

When you compute a patch metric, you'll get a value for every patch. This can be quite slow for large landscapes. As an example, let's compute the area of each patch. This is done with the `lsm_p_area()` function.

```{r}
res <- lsm_p_area(landscape)
res
```

We get all the areas in hectares (check the help file if you want to know the units) and the output is stored in a tibble. We can thus use the usual data frame techniques to extract values, for example to get the IDs of all the patches with an area bigger than 0.005 ha.

```{r}
res[res$class == 2 & res$value > 0.005, "id"]
```

Some species don't really like edge effects and thus avoid staying close to edges of a patch. In this case, the area of the patch is maybe not the best metric to use. Fortunately, there's another metric that computes the core area of each patch.

```{r}
res <- lsm_p_cai(landscape)
res
```

Let's visualize the core areas of the patches for all three classes separately using the `show_cores()` function.

```{r}
show_cores(landscape, class = "all")
```

Some functions, like `lsm_p_cai()` have additional arguments. For the core area index, we can specify the width of the edge using the `edge_depth` argument. The distance is specified in cell numbers.

```{r}
res <- lsm_p_cai(landscape, edge_depth = 2)
res
show_cores(landscape, class = "all", edge_depth = 2)
```

It is sometimes useful to show the values of the patch metrics on a map. This can also help to understand the results of more complex metrics. The `show_lsm()` function creates such a map in which the value of each pixel is equal to the associated patch metric.

```{r}
show_lsm(landscape, what = "lsm_p_area")
```

It is also possible to save this map as a `SpatRaster` object using the `spatialize_lsm()` function. The raster will be stored in a nested list. Only patch metrics are allowed.

```{r}
res <- spatialize_lsm(landscape, what = "lsm_p_area")
res[[1]][[1]]
```


## Class metrics

Class metrics put the focus on the different types of land cover. They're either directly based on the spatial structure of the classes or based on some statistical summary of the patch metrics distributions for each class. We can for example compute the proportions of the landscape that fall into each class using the `lsm_c_pland()` function.

```{r}
lsm_c_pland(landscape)
```

If we are more interested in the effect of edges, we can compute the edge density index with the `lsm_c_ed()` function. This index shows how many edge units of a given class are present per hectare of landscape.

```{r}
lsm_c_ed(landscape)
```

The following metric, the mean of perimeter-area ratio (`lsm_c_para_mn()`), is an example where we use a statistical summary of a patch metric distribution for each class. The patch metric is the so-called perimeter-area ratio. The ratio gets larger as the shape complexity of the patches increases. The metric is first computed for each patch and then averaged using the arithmetical mean.

```{r}
lsm_c_para_mn(landscape)
```

If we are more interested in the variability of the patch metric within each class, we can for example use the standard deviation instead of the mean.

```{r}
lsm_c_para_sd(landscape)
```

The `landscapemetrics` package offers functions to compute the mean, standard deviation and coefficient of variation of all the patch metrics. If you need another distribution statistic (e.g., median), you can easily compute the desired metric for each patch and then summarize the metric distribution per class using the function you need.


## Landscape metrics

```{r}
land_augusta <- rast(augusta_nlcd)
extent1 <- ext(c(xmin = xmin(land_augusta), xmax = xmax(land_augusta), ymin = ymin(land_augusta), ymax = 1253415))
extent2 <- ext(c(xmin = xmin(land_augusta), xmax = xmax(land_augusta), ymin = 1253415, ymax = ymax(land_augusta)))
land1 <- crop(land_augusta, extent1)
land2 <- crop(land_augusta, extent2)
```

Let's plot the two landscapes.

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(2, 1))
plot(land1, legend = FALSE)
plot(land2, legend = FALSE)
```

Shannon diversity index: lsm_l_shdi(), value of 0 when there's only a single patch in the landscape. If 2 landscapes have the same number of classes and one of them has a higher index, then we know this landscape has classes that are more evenly distributed.

```{r}
lsm_l_shdi(land1)
lsm_l_shdi(land2)
```

Contagion: lsm_l_contag (probability of two random cells belonging to the same class. Contagion is affected by both the dispersion and interspersion of classes. Shows how clumpy the landscape is, or how connected similar land cover types are across the area of interest). Close to 0 = different types are highly mixed and dispersed (fragmentation), close to 100 = opposite

```{r}
lsm_l_contag(land1)
lsm_l_contag(land2)
```


## Computing several indices

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
# Several metrics at the same time
calculate_lsm(landscape, what = c("lsm_c_pland", "lsm_l_ta", "lsm_l_te"), full_name = TRUE)
calculate_lsm(landscape, type = "aggregation metric", level = c("patch", "landscape"), full_name = TRUE)

metrics <- calculate_lsm(landscape, what = c("patch", "class"))
calculate_correlation(metrics, diag = FALSE)
show_correlation(metrics) # common to remove stuff with correlation 0.7 or higher
```


## Extracting and sampling indices

```{r}
# Extract (only for patch metrics)
pts <- matrix(c(10, 22, 22, 5, 26, 20), ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)
pts <- vect(pts, crs = "EPSG:2056")
plot(landscape)
plot(pts, col = "red", cex = 2, add = TRUE)
extract_lsm(landscape, y = pts, what = "lsm_p_area")

# Sample landscape metrics (y can be polygons, too)
sample_lsm(landscape, y = pts, size = 10, shape = "circle", what = c("lsm_l_msidi", "lsm_l_pr", "lsm_l_shei"))

# hide code
plot(landscape, ext = ext(landscape) + 6, box = FALSE, axes = FALSE, legend = FALSE)
plot(buffer(pts, width = 10), cex = 3, border = "red", add = TRUE)
plot(pts, col = "red", cex = 2, add = TRUE)

# Sample in several buffers
# creating buffers of 5 and 10 meters 
sizes = c(5, 10)

# calculating landscape metric for square buffers
library(purrr)
sizes |> 
  set_names() |> 
  map_dfr(~ sample_lsm(landscape, y = pts, what = "lsm_l_msidi", size = .), .id = "buffer_size")
```


## Focal analysis

```{r}
# Moving window (only for landscape metrics)
win <- matrix(1, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
win

res <- window_lsm(landscape, window = win, what = c("lsm_l_msidi", "lsm_l_pr", "lsm_l_shei"))
res
res <- rast(res[[1]])
plot(res)
```
```{r}
landcover <- rast(system.file("raster/landcover2015.tif", package = "motif"))
landcover_old <- rast(system.file("raster/landcover2001.tif", package = "motif"))

extent <- ext(c(xmin = 600000, xmax = 800000, ymin = -1100000, ymax = -800000))
land_new <- crop(landcover, extent)
land_old <- crop(landcover_old, extent)
```
```{r}
#| eval: false
win <- matrix(1, nrow = 5, ncol = 5)
# relative mutual information (relmutinf) metric, which quantifies the clumpiness of the landscape – the larger the value, the more clumped the landscape is
new <- window_lsm(test, window = win, what = "lsm_l_relmutinf")
old <- window_lsm(test_old, window = win, what = "lsm_l_relmutinf")
diffs <- old[[1]][[1]] - new[[1]][[1]]
# Areas where the clumpiness of the landscape has increased (positive values) and decreased (negative values)
plot(diffs)
```


## Motif

```{r}
library(motif)
library(sf)

landcover_comp <- lsp_signature(landcover, type = "composition", threshold = 1, normalization = "none")
landcover_comp
landcover_comp$signature

landcover_coma <- lsp_signature(landcover, type = "coma", window = 200)
landcover_coma

# Plot, hide code
stars200 <- lsp_add_sf(landcover, window = 200)
plot(landcover)
plot(st_geometry(stars200), add = TRUE)

# Search similar
extent <- ext(c(xmin = 238000, xmax = 268000, ymin = -819814, ymax = -789814))
landcover_cropped <- crop(landcover, extent)
plot(landcover_cropped)

search_1 <- lsp_search(landcover_cropped, landcover, type = "cove", dist_fun = "jensen-shannon", window = 100, threshold = 1)
search_1
plot(search_1["dist"], breaks = c(0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1.01))
search_1$id[which(search_1$dist < 0.001)]
search_1_690 <- lsp_extract(landcover, window = 100, id = 690)
plot(search_1_690)

# Compare (find areas with the largest changes of land cover spatial patterns)
compare_1 <- lsp_compare(landcover, landcover_old, type = "cove", dist_fun = "jensen-shannon", window = 100, threshold = 0.9)
plot(compare_1["dist"],breaks=c(0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1.01))
compare_1_max = max(compare_1$dist, na.rm = TRUE)
unique(compare_1$id[which(compare_1$dist == compare_1_max)])
compare_1_2036 = lsp_extract(c(landcover_old, landcover), window = 100, id = 2036)
plot(compare_1_2036[[1]], main = "2001")
plot(compare_1_2036[[2]], main = "2015")
```

One of the reason to start landscapemetrics was also to have a collection of metrics that are not included in FRAGSTATS. This vignette will highlight them and provide references for further reading on them. Information-theoretical framework can be applied to derive four metrics of landscape complexity: Marginal entropy [H(x)], Conditional entropy [H(y|x)], Joint entropy [H(x, y)], and Mutual information [I(y,x)]. https://r-spatialecology.github.io/landscapemetrics/articles/new_metrics.html

sample_lsm: percentage_inside: the size of the actual sampled landscape in %. It is not always 100% due to two reasons: (i) clipping raster cells using a buffer not directly intersecting a raster cell center lead to inaccuracies and (ii) sample plots can exceed the landscape boundary.
